title: Drawdown arithmetic and the protocol
teaches: A drawdown is how far the account is below its highest value, open trades included, checked at least weekly; every loss needs a bigger gain to repair (down 25% needs about 33%, down 50% needs 100%); our ladder cuts the max position as the drawdown deepens (normal cap 40%, then 10% at 6% down, 8% at 8%, 5% at 10%, no new trades at 15%), size comes back one rung each time half the drawdown is won back and the normal cap returns within 5% of the peak, and a monthly loss of 8% closes the month to new trades, with no daily or weekly limit.

facts.quote: A drawdown is typically quoted as the percentage difference between the peak of an investment and its following trough.
facts.claim: A drawdown is the percent drop from a peak to the low that follows it.

facts.quote: The drawdown would be calculated like this if an investment account of $20,000 dropped down to a value of $18,000 and then recovered to $20,000. The account experienced a 10% drawdown in this period:
facts.claim: An account that falls from $20,000 to $18,000 and then recovers has had a 10% drawdown.

facts.quote: This also demonstrates that a drawdown isn't always the same as a loss.
facts.claim: A drawdown is not always the same as your loss.

facts.quote: The XYZ stock experienced a drawdown of 27.3%, but the trader's unrealized loss at the $80 trough was $20 because they had purchased the stock at $100 per share, rather than the peak price of $110.
facts.claim: Drawdown runs from the peak ($110), while your loss runs from what you paid ($100), so the two differ.

facts.quote: If the price of XYZ stock then rises to a new peak of $120, drops to a new trough of $105, and then recovers to $120, that would be a new drawdown of $15 or 12.5%.
facts.claim: A stock bought at $100 that peaks at $120 and dips to $105 is in a 12.5% drawdown while still above cost.

facts.quote: The size of a drawdown is only one part of the measurement. Equally important is the time it takes to recover from a drawdown.
facts.claim: How long a drawdown takes to recover matters as much as how deep it is.

facts.quote: The primary risk associated with drawdowns is the uptick in share price needed to overcome that drawdown.
facts.claim: The main risk of a drawdown is the gain it takes to get back.

facts.quote: However, a fund that experiences a drawdown of 20% must recover significantly more of its share price to reach its peak again.
facts.claim: A 20% drawdown takes a much bigger climb to get back to the peak.

facts.quote: Maximum drawdown (MDD) is the largest decline in an investment's value from its peak to trough before a new peak is achieved.
facts.claim: Max drawdown is the biggest fall from a peak to a low before a new high.

facts.quote: The initial peak of $750,000 is used in the MDD calculation. The interim peak of $600,000 is not used, since it does not represent a new high.
facts.claim: A bounce that stays under the old high is not a new peak, so max drawdown still runs from the old high.

facts.quote: The MDD calculation takes into consideration the lowest portfolio value ($350,000 in this case) before a new peak is made, and not just the first drop to $400,000.
facts.claim: Max drawdown uses the lowest point before a new high, not just the first drop.

facts.quote: MDD only measures the largest loss size, not how often losses occur. MDD doesn't show how long recovery from the largest loss takes or if recovery happens.
facts.claim: Max drawdown shows how deep the worst fall was, not how long the recovery took or whether it came.

facts.quote: The largest cumulative percentage decline in the Net Asset Value of your portfolio from the highest or peak value to the lowest or trough value after the peak.
facts.claim: Max drawdown is the biggest percent fall in your account's value from its high to the low after it.

facts.quote: Ulcer Index measures the depth and duration of percentage drawdowns in price from earlier highs. The greater a drawdown in value, and the longer it takes to recover to earlier highs, the higher the UI.
facts.claim: Drawdowns run from earlier highs, and both their depth and the time to recover count.

facts.quote: For example a 50% loss requires a subsequent 100% gain to break-even. A given percentage loss always requires a greater percentage gain to break-even.
facts.claim: A 50% loss needs a 100% gain to get back to even, and every loss needs a bigger percent gain than itself.

facts.quote: Instead, many non-expert investors may assume for example that a 50% gain is sufficient to offset a 50% loss.
facts.claim: Many investors wrongly think a 50% gain makes up for a 50% loss.

facts.quote: While returns of +10% and –10% result in a total return of –1%, a return sequence of +50% and –50% results in a total return of –25%.
facts.claim: Up 10% then down 10% loses 1% overall; up 50% then down 50% loses 25%.

facts.quote: For returns of +/-50% a stock worth $100 increases to $150, before falling to $75.
facts.claim: Up 50% then down 50% turns $100 into $150, then $75.

facts.quote: The second percentage change multiplies both the initial value and the first percentage change.
facts.claim: Percent changes compound: each one applies to the value the last one left.

facts.quote: An unusual feature of percentage returns is that a subsequent 29.2% increase is required to reverse Black Monday's 22.6% decrease.
facts.claim: Black Monday's 22.6% drop needed a 29.2% gain to reverse.

facts.quote: For instance, to recover from a 10% loss, an investor needs an 11% gain. To recover from a 50% loss, an investor needs a 100% gain.
facts.claim: Down 10% needs about 11% back; down 50% needs 100% back.

facts.quote: The first contemporary global financial crisis unfolded on October 19, 1987, a day known as "Black Monday," when the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 22.6 percent.
facts.claim: On Black Monday, October 19, 1987, the Dow fell 22.6% in one day.

facts.quote: the S&P 500 index fell 57 percent from its October 2007 peak to its trough in March 2009.
facts.claim: The S&P 500 fell 57% from its October 2007 peak to its March 2009 low.

facts.quote: Reduce position size. Less money at risk equals less pressure and clearer thinking. Traders can then increase position size as they demonstrate a new track record of executing their system.
facts.claim: After a big loss, trade smaller, then size back up as you prove you are following your system again.

facts.quote: Regardless of how a trader processes a blowup, it's best to get back into the market gradually by employing one of the following tactics:
facts.claim: After a big loss, come back to the market gradually.

facts.quote: The combination of a heightened emotional state and shallow thinking can lead to typical bad behaviors, such as ignoring stops, selling winners too soon, and doubling down after a loss.
facts.claim: Doubling down after a loss is one of the typical bad behaviors after a big hit.

facts.quote: They can also implement "circuit breakers" to prevent additional trading after a certain level of loss in a day.
facts.claim: Some traders set a loss level that stops further trading for the day.

facts.quote: For example, they could pledge to step away for the day if they lose a certain amount of money or take 15 minutes if they feel an urge to break a trading rule.
facts.claim: Commit in advance to step away for the day after losing a set amount.

facts.quote: As a trader works to figure out what needs fixing, there's no harm in reducing the size of your trades. Once your results get back on track, you can increase your risk-taking.
facts.claim: In a losing streak, trade smaller while you find the problem, and size back up once results recover.

facts.quote: Losing streaks can happen to the best of us, but sometimes a bout of bad luck can actually reflect a problem with our trading strategy.
facts.claim: A losing streak can be bad luck, or a sign that something in the strategy is broken.

facts.quote: The anti-Martingale system allows forex and other traders to increase their position size after profitable trades and reduce it after losses. This approach aims to maximize profit while limiting exposure during downturns.
facts.claim: Cutting size after losses and adding it back after wins is meant to limit your exposure in a downturn.

facts.quote: When a gambler who uses this method experiences a loss, they immediately double the size of the next bet.
facts.claim: The martingale method doubles the bet after every loss.

facts.quote: This assumes that the gambler has an unlimited supply of money to bet or at least enough to make it to the winning payoff.
facts.claim: Doubling after every loss only works if you have unlimited money, or enough to last until the win.

facts.quote: If that isn't the case, just a few successive losses under this system could lead to losing everything you came with.
facts.claim: Without unlimited money, doubling after losses can wipe you out in a few losses in a row.

facts.quote: The issue is that there is no way to predict when that will happen, before or after you run out of money.
facts.claim: You can't know when a losing run will turn, so betting that it must turn soon can run you out of money first.

facts.quote: To recoup their capital, or to seek “revenge” on the market after a string of losing trades, they may try to make up profits wherever they can, usually by increasing the size and frequency of their trades.
facts.claim: After a string of losses, traders often try to win it back by trading bigger and more often.

facts.quote: While this practice often results in poor performance
facts.claim: That kind of revenge trading often leads to poor results.

facts.quote: Managing risk on individual trades will also reduce the likelihood of a large drawdown, in turn reducing the psychological pitfalls that come from such circumstances.
facts.claim: Controlling the risk on each trade makes a large drawdown less likely.

facts.quote: Other traders use a drawdown concept to set a daily loss limit. They establish a target maximum allowable loss, and if they reach that target during the day, they end their activities at that point.
facts.claim: Some traders set a daily loss limit and stop trading for the day when they hit it.

facts.quote: How you set your drawdown limit is not relevant here, but once you do have it, you should have the discipline to observe it.
facts.claim: Whatever loss limit you set, obey it once it's hit.

facts.quote: To determine the correct position size from this information, the investor simply needs to divide the account risk ($500) by the trade risk ($20). This means 25 shares can be bought ($500 / $20).
facts.claim: Size comes from the stop: the dollars you will risk divided by the risk per share.

facts.quote: I lowered my max sizing to 5% down from 10% which is down from 20%.
facts.claim: As my drawdown deepened, I cut my max position size from 20% to 10% to 5%.

facts.quote: After a 6% drawdown I immediately reduce to 10% max. After an 8% drawdown I reduce to 8% max. And after 10% drawdown I reduce to 5% max.
facts.claim: Our ladder: after a 6% drawdown the max position is 10%; after 8%, 8%; after 10%, 5%.

facts.quote: A drawdown is how far the account is below its highest value, open trades included, checked at least weekly.
facts.claim: Our definition: a drawdown is how far the account sits below its highest value, open trades counted, checked at least weekly.

facts.quote: On the way down: under 6% down, the normal cap (A7); 6% down, max position 10%; 8% down, 8%; 10% down, 5%; 15% down, no new trades (B13).
facts.claim: Our ladder down: under 6% the normal cap; at 6% down a 10% max position; at 8%, 8%; at 10%, 5%; at 15%, no new trades.

facts.quote: At a 15% drawdown, stop opening new trades and review before trading again.
facts.claim: At a 15% drawdown we stop opening new trades and review before trading again.

facts.quote: Size comes back one rung of the ladder each time the account recovers half of the drawdown; full size again once the account is back within 5% of its peak.
facts.claim: The way back: one rung up each time the account wins back half of the drawdown, and the normal cap once the account is within 5% of its peak.

facts.quote: A7. Max position 40% of the account (raised from 20-25% on 2026-11-09: "RAISE THE CAP TO 40% ACTUALLY. ESPECIALLY WITH EARLY TRIMS AT 3-5R THAT IS FINE.").
facts.claim: Our normal cap is 40% of the account, raised on 2026-11-09 from the old 20% to 25%.

facts.quote: B15. No daily loss limit. ("15, no.")
facts.claim: We have no daily loss limit.

facts.quote: No weekly loss limit; a monthly loss limit of 8%: at 8% down in a calendar month (from the month's starting value), no new trades for the rest of the month.
facts.claim: No weekly loss limit; at 8% down from the month's starting value, no new trades for the rest of the calendar month.

facts.quote: No losing-streak rule: size is cut only by the drawdown ladder, in percent (A8, B13, B14).
facts.claim: We have no losing-streak rule; only the drawdown ladder, in percent, cuts size.

facts.quote: A tight stop never justifies a bigger position than that: a gap can jump the stop.
facts.claim: A tight stop never earns a position above the cap, because a gap can jump the stop.

facts.quote: A stop order becomes a market order once the stop price is reached. The price you receive upon execution, though, could be markedly different than your stop price.
facts.claim: Once triggered, a stop is a market order and can fill far from the stop price.

facts.quote: the size is the SMALLER of the risk-based size and the position cap (A7, or the ladder's cap in a drawdown, A8).
facts.claim: Size from the stop, then cap it: the position is the smaller of the stop-based size and the cap, including the ladder's cap in a drawdown.

facts.quote: On the way back up: one rung up each time the account wins back half of the drawdown; the normal cap again once the account is within 5% of its peak (B14).
facts.claim: On the way back up a separate rule runs: one rung up for each half of the drawdown won back, and the normal cap within 5% of the peak.

facts.quote: D43. Recalculate the account value weekly or monthly and size every trade from it.
facts.claim: We size every trade from the account value as recalculated, weekly or monthly.

walkthroughs.title: Measured from the high
steps: Your drawdown is how far the account has dropped from its high, as a percent of that high.
Say an account at $20,000 drops to $18,000, then comes back. That was a 10% drawdown.
It runs from the peak, not from what you paid. So it isn't always the same as a loss.

walkthroughs.title: Losses cost more to fix
steps: Down 10%, you need about 11% to get back. Down 50%, you need 100%.
The gain gets earned on what's left. So it always has to be bigger than the loss was.
Up 50% then down 50% isn't even. $100 goes to $150, then $75. Keep your losers small.

walkthroughs.title: Our drawdown ladder, down and back up
steps: Check your drawdown at least weekly, open trades included. It sets how big you're allowed to go.
Under 6% down, the normal 40% cap. At 6% down, max position 10%. At 8%, 8%. At 10%, 5%.
At 15% down, no new trades. Stop and review before you trade again.
On the way back, one rung up each time you win back half the drawdown. Within 5% of the peak, normal cap.

questions.q: Your account made a new high last month and it's slid ever since. What does your drawdown measure?
choices: The drop from that high to the low
Your loss from what you first paid
questions.answer: The drop from that high to the low
questions.why: The drop from that high to the low after it. That's all it is. It starts at the peak, not at your cost, so you can be green on a stock and still be in one. It also isn't one bad day. A drawdown can build quietly over weeks, and that's exactly why we check it every week.
questions.lesson_line: Drawdown starts at the high, not at what you paid.

wrong.Your loss from what you first paid: That's your loss on the trade. Drawdown starts at the peak, and the two often differ.
wrong.Your average loss per trade: That's your typical loser. Drawdown is the whole slide from the high to the low.
wrong.Your worst single day: One day is only a piece of it. A drawdown can build over many days, from the high down.

questions.simple: It's the drop from your high to the low after it, so it starts at the peak, not your cost.

reasons: stable definition, three facts from two publishers

questions.q: You're up for the year, but you're below the high your account set last month. You're still in a drawdown.
questions.why: True. Drawdown runs from the high, not from where you started. Buy a stock at $100, watch it run to $120, then dip to $105. That's a 12.5% drawdown, and you're still above cost. Your account works the same way. Green on the year doesn't mean you haven't handed a chunk back. I want to know how much I've given back from the top, because that's the number that sets my size.
questions.lesson_line: Up on the year and in a drawdown can both be true.
questions.simple: True, drawdown runs from the high, so you can be up on the year and still be in one.

questions.q: A loser gets away from you and half the account is gone. Fill in what it takes to get back.
questions.sentence: Down 50%, you need a ___ gain just to get back to even.
questions.why: 100%. Half your money is gone, so the half that's left has to double. Down 10% only needs about 11% back. Down 50% needs 100%. Most people guess 50%, and that's the trap. The hole gets deeper faster than it looks. That's why I cut losers small and early. A small loss is cheap to fix. A big one can eat your year.
questions.lesson_line: Down 50%, you have to double just to get back to even.
questions.simple: 100%, because once half is gone, the half you have left has to double.

questions.q: Weekend review. Your account's high is $50,000 and it closed Friday at $42,500. What's your drawdown?
questions.why: 15%. $50,000 minus $42,500 is $7,500 off the high. $7,500 over the $50,000 peak is 0.15, so 15%. Always divide by the peak, never by the low. Divide by $42,500 and you get 17.6%, which makes it look worse than it is. Get this one right every week. It's the number that tells you what size you're allowed to trade.
questions.lesson_line: The drop from the high, divided by the high. That's your drawdown.
questions.simple: 15%, because the $7,500 drop is 15% of the $50,000 peak.

wrong.17.6%: You divided the $7,500 by the $42,500 low. Drawdown is always measured against the peak.
wrong.85%: That's how much of the peak you still have, not how much you gave back.

questions.q: You're down 10% from your account's high. You need about an 11% gain to get back to it.
questions.why: True. After a 10% loss you're working with less money, and the gain gets earned on that smaller pile. So it takes about 11%, not 10%. That gap looks tiny here. It doesn't stay tiny. Down 50% needs 100%. That's why I want my losses cut while they're still cheap.
questions.lesson_line: Cut losses while they're small. Small ones are cheap to fix.
questions.simple: True, because the gain is earned on a smaller account, so 10% down needs about 11% back.

questions.q: A rough quarter leaves you 25% under your account's high. What gain gets you back there?
questions.why: About 33%. Think of the high as $100. Down 25% leaves you $75, and you need $25 back on that $75. That's a third, about 33%. The gain always gets earned on the smaller account, so the climb back is steeper than the fall. It's also why we stop opening new trades at 15% down. We never want to be digging out of a hole this deep.
questions.lesson_line: Down 25% needs about 33% back. Every loss costs more to fix than it cost to take.

wrong.25%: That's the trap. 25% earned on the smaller account leaves you short of the high.
wrong.About 20%: Backwards. You need more back than you lost, never less.
wrong.About 50%: Too much. That's double the loss. A 25% hole needs about 33%.

questions.simple: About 33%, because the gain is earned on the smaller account left after the 25% drop.

questions.q: A stock runs up 50%, then gives back 50%. If you held the whole way, you're back to even.
questions.why: False. Run $100 through it. Up 50% takes it to $150. Down 50% takes that $150 to $75. You're down 25%, even though the two moves look the same size. The loss comes off the bigger number. That's why round-tripping a big winner hurts so much, and why I sell some into strength and trail the rest.
questions.lesson_line: Equal ups and downs don't cancel. You end up behind.
questions.simple: False, because the 50% loss comes off a bigger number, so $100 ends at $75.

questions.q: Rough couple of weeks. You're 6% off your account's high and a clean setup triggers. What's the most you put in it?
questions.why: 10% of the account. At 6% down I cut my max position to 10% right away. Under 6% down you get the normal 40% cap. So that's a big step down, and it's on purpose. When you're losing, something's off, you or the market. Smaller positions keep a bad stretch from turning into a deep hole while you figure out which.
questions.lesson_line: Deeper hole, smaller max position.

wrong.5% of the account: That's the rung at 10% down. At 6% down the max is 10%.
wrong.6% of the account: That mixes up your drawdown with your size. 6% down sets a 10% max.
wrong.40% of the account: That's the normal cap, for under 6% down. At 6% it drops to 10%.

questions.simple: 10%, because 6% off the high is where we cut the biggest position from 40% down to 10%.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A7, A8)

questions.q: You started the year at $40,000, ran it to $50,000, and you're at $45,000 now. What's your drawdown?
questions.why: 10%. Where you started doesn't matter here. The high does. $50,000 down to $45,000 is $5,000, and $5,000 over $50,000 is 10%. Sure, you're up on the year. Doesn't matter. You've given back 10% from the top, and that's the number we size from. On our ladder, 10% down means a 5% max position.
questions.lesson_line: Measure from the high, wherever you started the year.
questions.simple: 10%, because drawdown is measured from the $50,000 high, not the $40,000 start.

wrong.0%: Being up on the year doesn't zero it out. Drawdown runs from the $50,000 high.
wrong.11.1%: You divided by the $45,000 you have now. Divide by the peak.
wrong.12.5%: That's measured from the $40,000 start. Drawdown runs from the high.

questions.q: A bad stretch takes your account from $50,000 to $40,000. What gain gets you back to $50,000?
questions.why: 25%. You need $10,000 back, but you're earning it on $40,000, not $50,000. $10,000 over $40,000 is 25%. So a 20% drop takes a 25% climb. That's the math behind cutting size early. Every extra point you lose makes the way back steeper.
questions.lesson_line: Gains get earned on what's left. That's why every loss costs more to fix.
questions.simple: 25%, because the $10,000 climb back is earned on $40,000, the smaller amount.

wrong.80%: That's $40,000 over $50,000, how much you kept. It's not the gain you need.
wrong.125%: That's $50,000 over $40,000. Take off the 100% you already have and it's 25%.
wrong.500%: That's the whole account over the $10,000 drop. Not a return.

questions.q: Two traders both had a 20% max drawdown last year. That number tells you which one recovered faster.
questions.why: False. Max drawdown tells you how deep the worst hole was. It says nothing about how long the climb out took, or if it ever came. One trader might be back at the high a month later. The other might still be under it. So I look at two things in any drawdown: how deep, and how long. Both hurt.
questions.lesson_line: Ask two things about any drawdown: how deep, and how long.
questions.simple: False, because max drawdown only shows how deep the fall was, not how long the climb back took.

questions.story: Your account runs from $100,000 to $120,000, drops to $96,000, bounces to $110,000, then sinks to $90,000. Later it makes a new high at $130,000.
questions.q: What was your max drawdown over that stretch?
questions.why: 25%. The high that counts is $120,000. The bounce to $110,000 never got back above it, so it doesn't reset anything. The low that counts is $90,000, the lowest point before the new high. $120,000 minus $90,000 is $30,000, and $30,000 over $120,000 is 25%. The bounce is what fools people. It feels like a fresh start. It isn't, not until you make a new high.
questions.lesson_line: Max drawdown runs from the high to the lowest low before a new high.

wrong.About 18%: That's measured from the $110,000 bounce. A bounce under the old high isn't a new peak.
wrong.20%: That's only the first drop, $120,000 to $96,000. The low that counts is the lowest one before a new high.
wrong.10%: That's measured from your $100,000 start. Drawdown runs from the peak.

questions.simple: 25%, because it runs from the $120,000 high to the $90,000 low, and the bounce never made a new high.

deeper.trap: The bounce is the trap. A rally to $110,000 feels like a fresh start, so people measure from it. But it never beat the $120,000 high. Investopedia's own example works the same way. Its interim peak of $600,000 is not used, since it is not a new high. The low that counts is $350,000, not the first drop to $400,000.

questions.story: You're at your account's high, risking 2% of the account on each trade. Then the market turns, and you take ten full losers in a row.
questions.q: How far below your high are you now?
questions.why: About 18%. Each loss takes 2% of what's left, so you keep 0.98 of the account each time. Ten in a row leaves about 0.82, so you're about 18% down. Ten losers, each one just a single trade, and you're in a deep hole. That also puts you past our 15% line, so no new trades until you've reviewed. 2% is the most we'd ever risk on one trade, and most of the time we risk a lot less. A cold streak always comes.
questions.lesson_line: Your risk per trade sets how deep a cold streak can dig.

wrong.20%: That's 2% times ten off the starting account. Each loss comes off a smaller account, so it lands a bit under.
wrong.2%: That's one loss. Ten in a row stack up.
wrong.Well over 20%: The other way. Each 2% comes off less money, so ten losses land under 20%, not over.

questions.simple: About 18%, because each 2% loss comes off a smaller account, so ten of them add up to a bit under 20%.

questions.story: You're 7% off your account's high. Then an A+ shows up, our cleanest kind of setup, the kind we normally size up on. You love it.
questions.q: What's the most you can put in it?
questions.why: 10% of the account. At 7% down you're past the 6% rung, so your max is 10%. The 8% rung hasn't hit yet. How much you love the setup doesn't move the ladder, and that's the point. In a drawdown, your read is the thing in question. So take the A+ at 10% and let it prove you right.
questions.lesson_line: The ladder reads your drawdown, not how much you like the setup.

wrong.8% of the account: That rung starts at 8% down. You're at 7%, so the max is still 10%.
wrong.5% of the account: That's the rung at 10% down. You can go smaller, but the most here is 10%.
wrong.40% of the account: That's the normal cap, for under 6% down. At 7% down it's 10%.

questions.simple: 10%, because 7% down is past the 6% step but short of the 8% step, so the cap is 10%.

questions.q: Your account's $90,000, 10% off its high. A name you like triggers. How many dollars can go in it?
questions.why: $4,500. At 10% down our max position is 5% of the account, and 5% of $90,000 is $4,500. Use the account as it is today, not the old high. We size off the current value, recalculated weekly or monthly. Sizing off the high means betting money you don't have anymore.
questions.lesson_line: Find your rung first. Then turn the percent into dollars on today's account.
questions.simple: $4,500, because at 10% down our cap is 5%, and 5% of $90,000 is $4,500.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A8) and the reading that the cap is a percent of today's account

wrong.$900: That's a 1% risk number. Here you're capping the whole position.
wrong.$4,050: You took the 10% off twice. The $90,000 already has the drawdown in it.

questions.q: Lose, double the next bet to win it back, lose again, double again. A few losers in a row like that can blow up an account.
questions.why: True. That's the martingale, a gambler's system. It only works if you have unlimited money, or enough to last until the win shows up. You don't. You can't know when the streak ends, and the size grows faster than the account can take. A few losers in a row and it's over. In a drawdown we do the opposite. We go smaller, not bigger.
questions.lesson_line: Never double up to win a loss back. That's how a drawdown turns into a blowup.
questions.simple: True, because each loss doubles the next bet, so a short losing run can use up all your money.

questions.story: Before the open, you set a loss limit for the day. By midday your losses hit it. A setup you like starts to form.
questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Take it with a tighter stop
Stop, unless it's an A+ setup
Raise the limit and take it
questions.why: Stop trading for the day. Traders who use a daily loss limit end their trading when they hit it. A limit only works if you obey it, and no setup earns an exception. We don't use a daily limit ourselves, but the same discipline holds for any limit you set.
questions.lesson_line: Set the limit when you're calm. Obey it when you're not.

wrong.Take it with a tighter stop: You're still trading past your limit. A tighter stop doesn't change that you're done for the day.
wrong.Raise the limit and take it: A limit you move once it's hit isn't a limit. Once you have it, have the discipline to obey it.
wrong.Stop, unless it's an A+ setup: A limit with an exception for great setups isn't a limit. Once you have it, have the discipline to obey it.

questions.simple: Stop for the day, because a loss limit you set only works if you obey it once it's hit.

deeper.trap: The trap is the setup itself. A loss limit is set before the open, when you're calm. The moment it's hit is when a good setup is hardest to pass up. Schwab notes that a heightened emotional state leads to bad behaviors like ignoring stops and doubling down after a loss. Our own rules have no daily limit. Our limits are the drawdown ladder and a monthly loss limit.

reasons: touches B15 (we have no daily loss limit); the owner may want it out of this track

questions.q: Black Monday, October 19, 1987. The Dow drops 22.6% in one session. What gain does it need to get back to even?
questions.why: 29.2%. A 22.6% drop leaves 77.4 of every 100 points. Getting 22.6 back on 77.4 is 29.2%. That hole got dug in one session. That's why your size limits get set before the bad day, never during it. You can't size down after the gap.
questions.lesson_line: Every drop needs a bigger gain to undo it. Even a single day's.
questions.simple: 29.2%, because after a 22.6% drop the gain is earned on a smaller number, so it has to be bigger.

deeper.example: Newall's paper uses this very day to show a quirk of percent returns: a 22.6% decrease needs a 29.2% increase to reverse. The bigger the fall, the wider the gap. A 50% loss needs a 100% gain, double the size of the fall.

wrong.22.6%: That's the same percent as the loss. Earned on the smaller number, it falls short.
wrong.45.2%: That's double the loss. Too much. It needs 29.2%.

questions.q: The S&P 500 fell 57% from its October 2007 high to its March 2009 low. What gain did it need to get back?
questions.why: About 133%. A 57% fall leaves 43 of every 100. Getting 57 back on 43 is about 133%, more than a double. Down 50% already needs 100%, and every point past that gets steeper. Buy-and-hold sat through all of it. We don't have to. Our ladder cuts size as the hole deepens and stops new trades at 15% down. It's built to keep us out of a hole like that.
questions.lesson_line: Past 50% down, you need more than a double just to get back to even.

wrong.57%: The equal-percent trap. 57% on what was left falls way short of the old high.
wrong.About 100%: 100% fixes a 50% fall. This one was deeper, so the climb was steeper.
wrong.About 114%: That's double the 57% fall, and it's still short of the high.

questions.simple: About 133%, because a 57% fall leaves so little that it has to more than double to get back.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking in equal percents, or in doubles. A 57% gain on what was left falls far short, and even doubling the loss isn't enough.

reasons: computed key (calc gain_to_recover) on a historical number

questions.story: A cold month leaves you 8% below your account's high. Your last six trades were all losers.
questions.q: What's your next move?
choices: Trade smaller and find what's wrong
Trade more often to make it back
Press on, a win is due
questions.answer: Trade smaller and find what's wrong
questions.why: Trade smaller and find what's wrong. A streak can be bad luck or a broken strategy, so cut size while you check. Our ladder already caps a position at 8% of the account here.
questions.lesson_line: In a drawdown, shrink first and diagnose second.

wrong.Trade more often to make it back: That's revenge trading. Trading bigger and more often to win it back often ends in poor results.
wrong.Press on, a win is due: No win is ever due. There's no way to know when a streak ends, and betting that it must can run you out of money first.

questions.q: You're at your high, then you take ten losers in a row, each costing 2% of what's left. What gain gets you back to the high?
questions.why: 22%. Each loser leaves 0.98 of the account, and ten of them leave about 0.82. To get from 0.82 back to 1, you need about 1.22 times what you have. That's a 22% gain. Here's the funny part. The hole is a bit under 20%, but the climb out is over 20%. Losses shrink as the account shrinks, and the gain gets earned on the smaller account. Both point at one habit: keep risk per trade small.
questions.lesson_line: Ten 2% losses in a row need about a 22% gain to undo.
questions.simple: 22%, because ten 2% losses leave a smaller account, and the gain back is earned on that smaller amount.

deeper.trap: The trap is adding up the losses and calling that the gain you need. The hole is a bit smaller than the sum of the losses, because each 2% comes off less money. But the gain back is bigger than the hole, because it's earned on the smaller account. Those two effects pull opposite ways, and the gain needed ends up bigger than the sum.

wrong.20%: You added up ten 2% losses. The climb back is bigger than that.
wrong.18%: That's the size of the hole, not the climb back out.
wrong.25%: You treated it like a flat 20% drop. The real hole is a bit smaller, so the climb is too.

questions.story: Last month your account sank to 11% below its high, its lowest point. This month your five trades followed your plan and won, but they were small. It's still about 11% below the high.
questions.q: You've got your confidence back. What's your max position now?
questions.why: 5% of the account. You're still about 11% down, past the 10% rung, so the max is 5%. Five winners feel great. The ladder doesn't care how it feels. It reads the account in percent. A rung only comes back when you've won back half the drawdown, and small wins haven't done that yet. Keep stacking clean trades at 5%. The account will hand you the size back.
questions.lesson_line: Size comes back with the account, not with a hot streak.

wrong.8% of the account: That's one rung back. You earn it by winning back half the drawdown, not with a streak.
wrong.10% of the account: That's the cap at 6% down. You're about 11% down, so it's 5%.
wrong.40% of the account: That's the normal cap. It only comes back once you're within 5% of your peak.

questions.simple: 5%, because at about 11% down the cap is 5%, and a run of small wins doesn't change that.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading a hot streak as the all-clear. Schwab suggests sizing back up as you show a new track record. Our rule replaces that. The ladder reads the account in percent, and a rung comes back only when the account wins back half of the drawdown.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A8, B14, B17)
rewritten in the final check (streak vs account)
fixed in the cold check (house flag, month timing, facts trimmed)

questions.story: You're 8% below your account's high. You risk 1% a trade. Your best setup in months has an honest stop 5% below entry.
questions.q: How big is the position?
questions.why: 8% of the account. Start with the stop. 1% risk over a 5% stop says a 20% position. Then check the ladder. At 8% down, our max is 8%. The smaller number wins, so you take 8%, and your real risk drops under 1%. That's fine. In a drawdown you want less on, even on your best idea. And a 5% stop is the widest I'll take on anything.
questions.lesson_line: Size from the stop, then apply the ladder. The smaller number wins.

wrong.20% of the account: That's the stop math with no cap. At 8% down, the max is 8%.
wrong.1% of the account: 1% is your risk, not your position. Two different numbers.
wrong.10% of the account: That's the cap at 6% down. At 8% down it's 8%.

questions.simple: 8%, because at 8% down our cap is 8%, which is smaller than the 20% the stop math gives.

deeper.trap: The trap is trusting the stop math alone. Size from the stop is the first number, not the last: 1% risk over a 5% stop gives 20%. Then the ladder caps it. At 8% down the cap is 8%, so the position is 8% and the real risk is less than 1%. The best setup in months doesn't change the rung.

questions.q: You're holding a loser you haven't sold yet. It doesn't count toward your drawdown until you sell it.
questions.why: False. We count open trades. Your drawdown is how far the whole account sits below its high, open positions included. An unsold loser is already part of the hole. Telling yourself it isn't real until you sell is how people end up holding losers way too long. The market doesn't care what you've booked.
questions.lesson_line: Drawdown is measured on the whole account, open trades included.
questions.simple: False, because our drawdown counts the whole account, open trades included, so an unsold loser still counts.

questions.q: Busy week, and you haven't looked at your drawdown. How often should you be checking it, at the least?
questions.why: Once a week, at the least. More is fine. Drawdown counts open trades, so it moves even when you don't trade. And the ladder can only cut your size if you know the number. Put it in your weekend routine: account value, the high, the drawdown, then your max size for the week.
questions.lesson_line: Check the drawdown at least weekly. The ladder can only work on a number you've looked at.

wrong.After every trade: You can, but trades aren't the trigger. Once a week is the floor, trade or no trade.
wrong.Once every month: Too slow. A lot can slip in a month before the ladder ever kicks in.
wrong.After a losing run: We don't have a streak rule. The ladder runs on the drawdown percent, checked weekly no matter what.

questions.simple: Once a week, because the ladder can only cut your size if you know the number.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A8, B17)

questions.q: Your account keeps sliding. Fill in the line where you stop opening trades.
questions.sentence: At a ___ drawdown we stop opening new trades and review.
questions.why: 15%. Short of 15% down, the ladder only shrinks your size: 10% max at 6% down, 8% at 8%, 5% at 10%. At 15% there's no size small enough. No new trades. You step back and review. Bad luck or something broken in how you trade, you find out which before money goes back to work.
questions.lesson_line: At 15% down the ladder ends in a stop: no new trades, review first.
questions.simple: 15%, because at 15% down our ladder goes from cutting size to no new trades until you review.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A8, B13)

questions.q: We have a daily loss limit. Lose a set amount in a day and you're done trading until tomorrow.
questions.why: False. No daily limit, and no weekly one either. What protects us is the drawdown ladder, read from the account's high, and a monthly limit. Lose 8% from where the month started and the month's closed to new trades. A bad day on its own doesn't stop us. A hole in the account does, and the ladder and the month catch it.
questions.lesson_line: No daily or weekly limit. The ladder and the 8% monthly limit do the job.
questions.simple: False, because we have no daily loss limit, only the drawdown ladder and an 8% monthly limit.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B15, B16, B17)

questions.q: November starts with your account at $60,000. At what value does the monthly loss limit close the month to new trades?
questions.why: $55,200. Our monthly limit is 8% down from where the month started. 8% of $60,000 is $4,800, and $60,000 minus $4,800 is $55,200. Hit it and you're done opening trades until next month. Write the number down when the month opens. You don't want to be doing math when you're down and frustrated.
questions.lesson_line: Monthly limit: 8% down from where the month started, and the month's closed to new trades.
questions.simple: $55,200, because our limit is 8% below the $60,000 the month started at.

wrong.$64,800: You added the 8%. The limit is 8% down, not up.
wrong.$59,520: Decimal slip. You took a tenth of the 8% off.
wrong.$65,217: You divided $60,000 by what's left. Take 8% off instead: $4,800 off $60,000.

questions.story: Your account peaked at $100,000 and sank to $88,000, a 12% drawdown, so your max position fell to 5%. It has climbed back to $94,000.
questions.q: What's your max position now?
questions.why: 8% of the account. The fall ran from $100,000 to $88,000, and $94,000 is halfway back. Half won back earns one rung, from 5% up to 8%. You don't jump straight to 10% just because you're now 6% off the high. The way back up runs on its own rule, one rung for each half won back. It makes you prove it with real money before the size comes back.
questions.lesson_line: The way back is one rung at a time: half the drawdown won back, one rung up.

wrong.5% of the account: That was the cap at the low. Winning back half the drawdown earns one rung back.
wrong.10% of the account: That reads today's drawdown off the way-down rungs. On the way back, half won back earns one rung: 5% to 8%.
wrong.40% of the account: The normal cap returns within 5% of the peak. At $94,000 you're still more than 5% below $100,000.

questions.simple: 8%, because $94,000 wins back half of the drop to $88,000, and half back earns one rung.

deeper.example: Check it. The drop from $100,000 to $88,000 is the drawdown, and half of it brings the account back to $94,000. That earns one rung: from 5% to 8%. The normal cap of 40% waits until the account is within 5% of its peak.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B14) and a reading of 'half of the drawdown' the owner has not confirmed

questions.q: Your account's high is $80,000 and you fell 10% from it. At what value do you get your full position cap back?
questions.why: $76,000. The full cap comes back once you're within 5% of the peak. 5% of $80,000 is $4,000, and $80,000 minus $4,000 is $76,000. You don't need a new high to trade full size again. You do need to win most of it back with real trades first. Size follows the account, not your mood.
questions.lesson_line: Full size again within 5% of the peak. Not at the peak, not at the first green week.
questions.simple: $76,000, because the normal cap comes back within 5% of the $80,000 peak.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B14) and the reading that exactly 5% down counts as within 5%

wrong.$72,000: That's 10% off the peak, the size of the fall. That's where you were, not where the cap returns.
wrong.$4,000: That's the 5% gap in dollars, not the account value.
wrong.$68,400: You took 5% off the fallen $72,000. Measure from the peak.

questions.story: You're at your account's high, risking 1% a trade. A setup you love has its stop just 1% under the entry, so the stop math says a 100% position.
questions.q: How much do you actually put in it?
questions.why: 40% of the account. That's our cap, and a tight stop never earns more. The stop math says 100%, but the size is the smaller of the two. Here's why. A stop turns into a market order once it's hit. If the stock gaps down overnight, you get filled wherever it opens, not at your stop. With the whole account in one name, one gap can wreck your year. With 40% on, it hurts, but you're still here.
questions.lesson_line: The cap is 40%. A tight stop shrinks the risk math, never the cap.

wrong.100% of the account: That's the stop math with no cap. A 1% stop can get gapped right through.
wrong.20% of the account: That was the old max. The cap is 40% now.
wrong.10% of the account: That's the cap at 6% down. You're at the high, so it's 40%.

questions.simple: 40%, because that's our cap, and a tight stop can't lift it since a gap can jump the stop.

deeper.trap: The trap is a tight stop. Risk math divides your risk by the stop distance, so a 1% stop turns 1% risk into a 100% position. But a stop becomes a market order once hit, and the fill can be far from the stop price. A gap through a 1% stop on a 100% position can cost far more than the 1% you planned. That's why the 40% cap holds whatever the stop says.

questions.story: A brutal quarter. Your account peaked at $100,000 and is $85,000 today, open positions included. A clean setup triggers today.
questions.q: What do you do with it?
choices: Take it, but at a 5% max position
Take it, the ladder only caps size
questions.why: No new trades, review first. $100,000 down to $85,000 is 15%, open positions counted. That's the line. Short of 15%, the ladder only shrinks your size. At 15% it stops you. You don't have to sell what you hold. You just don't open anything new. Then you sit down and figure out if this was bad luck or something broken in how you're trading. A clean setup on that day is exactly what tests you.
questions.lesson_line: At 15% down, the answer to any setup is no. Review, then earn the way back.

wrong.Take it, the ladder only caps size: Short of 15% down it only caps size. At 15% it stops you.
wrong.Take it, but at a 5% max position: 5% is the rung for 10% down. At 15% there's no size, just no new trades.
wrong.Close every open position today: The rule stops new trades and asks for a review. It doesn't make you sell what you hold.

questions.simple: No new trades, because the fall from $100,000 to $85,000 hits our 15% line, so you review first.

deeper.trap: The trap is treating 15% like one more rung. Short of 15% down, each rung only shrinks the max position, so a smaller trade still fits. At 15% there is no smaller size: the answer to any setup is no until you've reviewed. A clean setup that day is exactly what tests the rule.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A8, B13)

questions.story: Your account peaked at $100,000 in the summer. It started this month at $95,000 and sits at $87,000 today, 13% below the peak.
questions.q: What stops you from opening new trades today?
questions.why: The monthly limit. $95,000 down to $87,000 this month is more than 8%, so the month's closed to new trades. The ladder alone wouldn't stop you. 13% down is short of the 15% line, so it only caps you at 5%. Two clocks run at once: the ladder from the peak, the monthly limit from the month's start. Either one can stop you, so check both.
questions.lesson_line: Two clocks run at once: the ladder from the peak, the 8% limit from the month's start. Either can stop you.

wrong.The 15% drawdown stop: You're 13% below the peak, short of the 15% line. The ladder caps you at 5%. The month is what stops you.
wrong.The daily loss limit: We don't have a daily limit. The monthly one is what bites here.
wrong.Nothing stops you today: The ladder alone would let you trade at a 5% max. But the month's down more than 8%, and that closes it.

questions.simple: The monthly limit, because the account fell more than 8% from the $95,000 it started the month at.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading only one clock. The ladder runs from the peak: 13% below $100,000 caps a position at 5% but doesn't stop you. The monthly limit runs from the month's start. From $95,000 to $87,000 is more than 8%, and that closes the month to new trades. Either clock can stop you, so check both.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A8, B13, B15, B16)

Schwab, "How to Recover From a Big Trading Loss" (Joe Mazzola, 2026-03-09, schwab.com/learn/story/how-to-recover-from-big-trading-loss): suggests cutting from risking "5%" of the portfolio per trade to "2% or 3%" after a big loss, and adding to a new position "anytime the price dips". Both clash with our 2% ceiling (F9.01) and with not averaging down, and the page leans on tax write-offs (no taxes in Study).
